newsitem.title: USA: No big changes in U.S.-U.K. ties foreseen.
newsitem.headline: No big changes in U.S.-U.K. ties foreseen.

text.p: Some see President Bill Clinton and Britain's Labour party leader Tony Blair as trans-Atlantic twins, while Clinton and defeated Conservative leader John Major often seemed like polar opposites.
But few in Washington think there will be a dramatic change in relations between the United States and Britain as Blair takes over from Major as the new prime minister after Thursday's election.
U.S. and British interests are too similar and their longstanding "special relationship" too unique to be held hostage to mere changes in government, many U.S. analysts say.

"It strikes me that Bill Clinton may find something of a soul mate in Tony Blair. Certainly he did not have a close personal relationship with John Major, who made no secret of his preference for (former president) George Bush," said Allan Lichtman, a political historian with American University.
"But I do think the relationship between the United States and Britain transcends ideology and parties," Lichtman said.

"I don't think the underlying relations are going to change all that much," said Helmut Sonnenfeldt, a Brookings Institution scholar and a foreign policy adviser in the administrations of John Kennedy, Lyndon Johnson and Richard Nixon.

"In general, on broad policy questions the U.S. and the British are the same. Unless some rabidly left-wing Labour person shows up and wields a lot of influence, the relationship will not be affected much," Sonnenfeldt said.

Before Clinton ever got to the White House, he had trouble with some in Major's party. Some Conservative strategists advised Clinton's opponent, then-President George Bush, in the 1992 presidential campaign.
If the president was irritated, history then gave him a chance to return the favour by welcoming Irish nationalist Gerry Adams to the United States.
Two years ago, after Adams received a U.S. visa allowing him to raise funds in the United States, an annoyed Major refused to return a call from Clinton for an entire week.
Blair, meanwhile, has been portrayed -- sometimes unflatteringly -- as a Clinton "clone" by some U.S. media.

Like Clinton, Blair is a young politician of the post-Second World War generation who sought to move his party from the left to the centre of the political spectrum. Blair is 43; Clinton was 46 when he took office.

Some Democratic strategists who worked for Clinton have been advising the Labour campaign in Britain. "This election will be the final nail in the coffin of the conservative Reagan-Thatcher era," said one, Bob Mulholland, a California Democrat, referring to former President Ronald Reagan and former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher.
The White House minimised the differences with Major, while resisting the description of Blair as a Clinton copy.

"The personal relationship that Major and Clinton had is much closer than is commonly perceived. We worked together so closely with him that it's hard to see a real change" under a Labour government, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said.

"One would expect continuity first and foremost" with Blair, he added. The major foreign policy issue in the campaign was Britain's relationship with the European Union, McCurry said, "and that has less to do with the United States than with how Britain relates to other European countries."

There have been but a handful of foreign policy issues in recent years in which U.S. and British officials have openly differed. Northern Ireland was one, and how to end the war in Bosnia was another, although in both cases the governments now appear to be singing from the same hymnbook.

An Irish official in Washington said Labour's victory in Britain could provide a new opportunity for a cause important to Clinton: the Northern Ireland peace process. It has stalled over the Irish Republican Army's refusal to call a ceasefire in its war against British rule of the province.

"I think it (a Labour victory) provides a new opportunity psychologically for everyone to try to come back to the process," the Irish official said, adding: "The Clinton administration presumably will want to see early progress and this could make it a priority for Blair."
But Sonnenfeldt said Blair, in general, might want to be careful not to appear too anxious to please Clinton.

"We'll see how much they really like each other when they rub elbows," Sonnenfeldt said. "Blair has to watch himself that he doesn't look like a Clinton clone, a Clinton puppy, because the press will get after him if he does."
